## 2. Exact residues and an integral polynomial gauge

At r=1, a=4; at r=-1, a=-4. Since H_b(1)=1 and
(1-r^2)'=-2r, the differential d dr has residue 2 at BOTH points.
The residues are independent of g and of the original prime.

    ell=-4r/(1-r^2), ell dr=2 dlog(1-r^2),
    P_b(r)=d-ell=[4r-a H_b(r^2)]/(1-r^2).                (3)

The numerator vanishes at r=+1 and -1 over O. Its division by 1-r^2
is therefore an O-polynomial, without any p division. It is odd,
and has degree at most 2p-3: deg a=p, deg H_b(r^2)<=p-1, then the
division removes two degrees. Define the completely known polynomial

    Q_b(0)=0, Q_b'=P_b,
    Q_b=sum_j [r^j]P_b * r^(j+1)/(j+1).                 (4)

Only odd j occur, with j<=2p-3. Thus j+1 is even and lies between
2 and 2p-2. The only positive multiple of p in that interval is the
odd integer p, so every divisor in (4) is a p-unit. Consequently
Q_b belongs to O[r], is even, and has degree <=2p-2.

With v=V-Q_b z, (2) becomes (1). This is an explicit integral gauge
using ONLY the already specified baseline; it neither computes T nor

ell dr has residue 2e, which is nonzero in characteristic zero.
A derivative dh of a meromorphic algebraic function has zero residue:
in a local Laurent expansion, a term with differential exponent -1
would have to come from exponent zero, whose derivative is zero.
Therefore ell dr is not exact in L. This argument also applies at -1.

If the rank-two system became constant in L, one of a horizontal

That z is a nonzero differential constant, so its ratio v/z would
